strengths: Novel and well-motivated diffusion framework that unifies simplex-based and embedding-based text diffusion by smoothing over semantic distances; the paper explicitly proves (Appendix C) that simplex diffusion is a special case under a trivial metric, giving the approach a clean theoretical grounding.

Theorem 4.1 provides a practical and non-trivial simplification: instead of regressing the high-dimensional, high-variance D0 (distance vector over the vocabulary), the model can be trained to predict token embeddings directly, with a proof that this yields an equivalent optimum up to a constant shift that is irrelevant after softmax.

Extensive and fairly controlled experiments: four seq2seq datasets (XSum, Quasar-T, Newsela-Auto, QQP), reimplementation of embedding- and simplex-based diffusion variants under identical architecture/training budget for an apples-to-apples comparison, plus a battery of ablations (decoder complexity, number of denoising steps, stochasticity parameter δ̃, self-conditioning).
Mean-rank analysis across datasets shows SMOOTHIE achieves the best aggregate ranking while using fewer denoising steps than most baselines, which is a meaningful efficiency argument.
Clear writing, intuitive illustrations (Fig. 1), and an honest limitations section discussing fixed pretrained embeddings and fixed sequence length as concrete avenues for improvement.
weaknesses: Empirical superiority is inconsistent: SMOOTHIE underperforms the simplex-based variant on Quasar-T (Table 3, BLEU/ROUGE-L), underperforms DiffuSeq/SeqDiffuSeq on Newsela-Auto (Table 4), and always trails BART/FLAN-T5; the abstract's claim of outperforming 'existing diffusion-based models... on the majority of tasks' is only loosely supported when inspecting per-metric results rather than aggregated rankings.

No statistical significance testing, confidence intervals, or multiple random seeds are reported for any metric, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains (often 0.3–1.5 points) are meaningful versus noise.

No human evaluation is conducted despite the paper concerning open-ended text generation quality, where automatic metrics like BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore are known to be imperfect proxies for fluency and coherence.

Sensitivity of the method to key hyperparameters (σmin, σmax, d, δ, δ̃) is under-explored; only δ̃ is ablated (on a single unconditional dataset, ROCStories), while the noise-schedule shape parameters are fixed across all tasks without justification or sensitivity analysis.

Scale is limited to ~100M-parameter models trained from scratch; no comparison to larger or pretrained-initialized diffusion LMs (the paper explicitly excludes the pretrained TESS variant), leaving open how the method scales or compares against stronger baselines.
The mean-rank table excludes XSum, which somewhat cherry-picks the aggregate comparison in the paper's favor and reduces transparency of the overall summary claim.

Computational cost analysis is incomplete: while step count is reported, wall-clock/inference-time comparisons against baselines (especially simplex diffusion trained with cheaper cross-entropy loss) are not provided, despite efficiency being highlighted as an advantage.

strengths: The paper addresses a well-motivated problem: combining semantic-awareness of Gaussian/embedding diffusion with the discreteness-preserving property of simplex diffusion, and clearly frames the trade-off in Table 1.
The theoretical derivation (Theorem 4.1 relating the D0-space MSE objective to embedding-space MSE) is a nice technical contribution that makes training more tractable, and the proof appears correct.
The paper shows that the simplex diffusion approach is a special case of the proposed distance-based approach under a trivial metric (Appendix C), providing a clean unifying perspective.

Reasonably thorough ablations are included: importance of the reverse-process noise variance delta-tilde, decoder complexity ablation, denoising steps sensitivity, and controlled re-implementation of embedding/simplex baselines under the same architecture for fair comparison.
Evaluation spans four diverse seq2seq tasks (summarization, question generation, simplification, paraphrase) with multiple standard metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, SARI, diversity).
weaknesses: The core empirical claim that SMOOTHIE 'outperforms existing diffusion-based models' is inconsistently supported: on Quasar-T, the re-implemented Simplex baseline actually beats SMOOTHIE on BS, BLEU, and R-L; on Newsela-Auto, DiffuSeq and SeqDiffuSeq clearly outperform SMOOTHIE by large margins (e.g., BLEU 37.1 vs 19.9). The paper acknowledges these losses but the abstract/conclusion overstate the generality of the improvement.

The 'mean rank' analysis (Table 5) that is used to claim SMOOTHIE's overall superiority is computed over only 3 of 4 datasets and only among a subset of methods that have complete metric coverage, which appears to be a somewhat cherry-picked aggregation; XSum is excluded, and not all baselines (e.g., TESS, AR-Diffusion, GENIE) are included in the ranking despite being reported elsewhere in the paper.

Results are taken from multiple different prior papers with different implementations/training setups for the 'external' baselines (⋄ marked), while SMOOTHIE and re-implemented Embedding/Simplex baselines use a different, custom architecture — this makes head-to-head comparisons across the ⋄ vs ⋆ groups not fully controlled, weakening the fairness of the overall comparison narrative.

The improvement margins over the re-implemented Embedding/Simplex baselines (the most controlled comparison) are often small (e.g., BS 62.4 vs 62.0/63.0 on Quasar-T; 68.0 vs 65.6/62.1 on XSum), and no statistical significance or variance across seeds is reported, making it hard to assess whether gains are robust or within noise.

The method depends on frozen pre-trained BERT embeddings rather than end-to-end learned embeddings (acknowledged as a limitation), which could bias the Euclidean semantic space hypothesis assumption and may not generalize to other domains/tokenizers; no experiments test sensitivity to embedding choice.

The computational cost/efficiency comparison (e.g., wall-clock time, memory) between SMOOTHIE and baselines is not reported beyond number of denoising steps, despite the D0 vector having dimensionality proportional to vocabulary size V, which could be a substantial overhead not fully analyzed.

The paper's positioning of 'SMOOTHIE' as more principled than TESS/SSD-LM is undercut by their own results showing the simplex variant sometimes wins, and there is limited discussion/insight into why the theoretically motivated semantic-aware approach fails to consistently beat the semantics-agnostic simplex approach, which is a central and somewhat unresolved tension in the paper's narrative.

The human evaluation is absent; all quality assessments rely on automatic metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, SARI, diversity), which are known to have limitations in capturing fluency and semantic adequacy, especially in generative text tasks with legitimate diverse outputs (e.g., paraphrase, summarization).

strengths: The paper is well-motivated: it clearly identifies a real gap (Gaussian embedding diffusion respects semantics but not discreteness; simplex diffusion respects discreteness but not semantics) and proposes a principled way to unify both by diffusing over a vector of Euclidean distances to all vocabulary embeddings.

Solid theoretical grounding: Theorem 4.1 (with proof in Appendix D) justifies replacing a high-dimensional, high-variance D0 loss with a lower-dimensional embedding-prediction loss, and Appendix C rigorously shows that simplex diffusion is a special case of the proposed framework under a trivial metric, giving the method conceptual generality.

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation across four diverse seq2seq tasks (summarization, question generation, simplification, paraphrase) against many diffusion and autoregressive baselines, with a controlled, apples-to-apples re-implementation of embedding- and simplex-based diffusion under the identical architecture/training budget, which strengthens the causal claim that the latent space choice matters.

Useful ablations: the importance of the reverse-process noise scale delta-tilde for controlling the fluency/diversity trade-off, the negligible benefit of a complex context-aware decoder (contrasting with prior embedding-diffusion findings), and the effect of number of denoising steps per task complexity add practical insight beyond the headline numbers.
Practical efficiency benefit: SMOOTHIE achieves competitive/best mean rank while using markedly fewer denoising steps (2-10x) than several baselines.
Limitations section is honest and specific (frozen pretrained embeddings limiting scalability/quality; fixed sequence length inefficiency), rather than boilerplate.
weaknesses: Results are inconsistent across tasks: SMOOTHIE is outperformed by the simplex variant on Quasar-T and by SeqDiffuSeq/DiffuSeq on Newsela-Auto, and the overall margin of improvement (e.g., mean rank 2.0 vs. SeqDiffuSeq's 2.67) is fairly modest given the added architectural/theoretical complexity, weakening the significance claim that the method is uniformly better.

Baseline numbers are pulled from multiple different papers/protocols (noted explicitly in Sec 5.2) rather than uniformly reproduced, which introduces potential confounds (different tokenizers, training budgets, hyperparameter tuning) when comparing against DiffuSeq, SeqDiffuSeq, SSD-LM, TESS, AR-Diffusion, GENIE, and the autoregressive models; only the embedding/simplex ablation baselines are controlled experiments.

No human evaluation or statistical significance testing (e.g., confidence intervals, multiple seeds) is reported despite diffusion sampling being inherently stochastic, making it hard to assess whether reported gains (often 0.5-1 points in BERTScore/BLEU) are robust or within noise.

The method depends on a frozen, pretrained (BERT) embedding matrix rather than end-to-end learned embeddings; the paper acknowledges this may cap quality but does not empirically probe how sensitive results are to the choice or freezing of the embedding space, despite the whole method's core intuition (Euclidean semantic space hypothesis) resting on that embedding's quality.

Scale is limited to ~100M-parameter models trained from scratch on single-task datasets; no evidence is given that the smoothing diffusion idea scales to larger models/pretraining regimes, which is important since most modern text-diffusion interest is in scaling behavior.

The core technical idea is an incremental combination of two existing lines of work (heat-dissipation/blurring diffusion for images and simplex diffusion for text) rather than a fundamentally new mechanism; while the unification and theoretical connection are valuable, the degree of originality is moderate.

strengths: Well-motivated unification of embedding-space and simplex-space diffusion: representing tokens via vectors of distances to all vocabulary embeddings naturally interpolates between the two paradigms, and the paper formally proves (Appendix A) that simplex diffusion is a special case of SMOOTHIE under a trivial metric, giving the method a principled theoretical grounding.

Solid theoretical contributions beyond the main idea: a full ELBO derivation (Appendix B) and Theorem 4.1 (with proof in Appendix C) that justifies training with a simpler embedding-prediction loss instead of directly regressing the high-dimensional/high-variance distance vector, which is both elegant and practically useful.

Extensive and carefully controlled experiments across five diverse tasks (unconditional ROCStories, XSum summarization, Quasar-T question generation, QQP paraphrasing, ParaDetox detoxification), plus an additional large-scale OpenWebText experiment in the appendix, compared against a wide range of diffusion and autoregressive baselines.

Fair, apples-to-apples ablation: the authors reimplement embedding- and simplex-based diffusion within the same architecture/training pipeline to isolate the effect of the latent space choice, which is methodologically rigorous and strengthens the causal claim that the smoothing space itself is beneficial.

Thorough set of additional ablations (δ̃ stochasticity, noise scheduler shape, embedding choice, self-conditioning, number of denoising steps, and a new sampling solver vs. DDPM/DDIM) that collectively provide good insight into what drives performance and support reproducibility.
Detailed hyperparameter tables and dataset statistics in the appendix, and a promise to release code, supporting reproducibility.

Honest and specific limitations section discussing the reliance on fixed pretrained embeddings and the O(V×d) computational overhead of the distance computation, including why naive mitigations (e.g., top-k truncation) do not work.
weaknesses: The empirical gains over the embedding- and simplex-based diffusion ablations are often small and inconsistent across metrics (e.g., on Quasar-T BERTScore differs by ~1 point and ROUGE-L is actually worse than Simplex; on QQP diversity metrics are lower than both baselines), which somewhat weakens the central claim that the proposed latent space is clearly superior rather than marginally competitive.

The proposed sampling solver (Eq. 9), which ignores the previous latent state, is presented mainly as an empirical finding; the paper explicitly acknowledges a lack of theoretical understanding for why it outperforms DDPM/DDIM, leaving a potentially important design choice unexplained and somewhat ad hoc.

Computational cost is a real practical concern: the O(batch × seq_len × d × V) distance computation makes SMOOTHIE and simplex diffusion 1.75× slower than embedding diffusion, and the authors themselves note that straightforward mitigations (e.g., top-k approximation) are ineffective, raising scalability questions for larger vocabularies not fully explored (only one large-scale OpenWebText run is provided, in the appendix, at reduced scope).

The method depends on a fixed pretrained embedding matrix (BERT) rather than end-to-end learned embeddings; the paper acknowledges this may cap quality and defers resolution of embedding collapse/explosion issues to future work, leaving open how much of a limiting factor this really is.

No human evaluation is conducted; all quality assessments rely on automated metrics (BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, MAUVE, generative perplexity), which can be limited proxies for actual text quality/fluency, especially for tasks like summarization or detoxification.

The core idea of gradually removing information via Gaussian-kernel smoothing over a structured space is conceptually similar to prior heat-dissipation/blurring diffusion work in the image domain (Rissanen et al. 2023; Hoogeboom & Salimans 2023) that the paper explicitly cites as inspiration; the main novelty is the adaptation to token embedding distances, which, while sensible, is an incremental (though well-executed) extension rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

The Euclidean semantic space hypothesis underlying the method's motivation is taken largely on faith from a single citation (Hashimoto et al., 2016) without further empirical validation specific to the embeddings/tasks used in this paper.

strengths: The core idea—representing tokens via a vector of (negative squared) distances to all vocabulary embeddings and diffusing that representation—is a clean and well-motivated way to interpolate between Gaussian embedding diffusion (semantic-aware but requiring an explicit decoding step) and simplex diffusion (discreteness-respecting but semantically blind). The formal proof (Appendix A) that simplex diffusion is a special case of the proposed framework under a trivial metric is a nice theoretical contribution that clarifies the relationship between prior approaches.

Theorem 4.1, which shows that optimizing an embedding-prediction MSE objective is equivalent (up to a constant shift that is irrelevant after softmax) to optimizing the much higher-dimensional D0 prediction objective, is a useful and non-trivial simplification that makes training tractable; the proof appears correct.

The experimental protocol re-implements embedding- and simplex-based diffusion baselines within the authors' own architecture/training pipeline to isolate the effect of the latent space itself from confounds of architecture or training recipe, which is a methodologically sound way to support the central claim about the diffusion space.

The paper includes an unusually extensive set of ablations (noise scheduler, embedding choice, self-conditioning, solver comparison DDPM/DDIM vs. proposed solver, number of denoising steps, delta-tilde sensitivity, training dynamics, OpenWebText scale-up), which aids reproducibility and gives a reasonably complete picture of the method's behavior.

The proposed non-Markovian sampling scheme (Eq. 9), which ignores the previous latent state, is shown to consistently (if modestly) outperform DDPM/DDIM across all four seq2seq datasets, a useful practical finding even though its theoretical explanation remains speculative.
weaknesses: The empirical superiority of SMOOTHIE over prior methods is inconsistent and often marginal rather than clearly established. For example, on XSum, TEncDM achieves a higher BERTScore (69.9) than SMOOTHIE (68.8), and on Quasar-T, Simplex* has a higher ROUGE-L (36.9) than SMOOTHIE (36.5); the text's claim that 'SMOOTHIE consistently outperforms' is not fully supported by the tables presented.

Most reported metrics appear to be single-run results (only MAUVE is averaged over 5 seeds), so there is no indication of variance or statistical significance, making it hard to assess whether the reported gains over Embedding*/Simplex*/TEncDM are meaningful or within noise, especially given how small many of the differences are (e.g., 0.1 BERTScore points).

The method requires computing pairwise distances to the entire vocabulary at every denoising step, which the authors acknowledge is a real scalability bottleneck (Sec. 6) that cannot be easily mitigated by top-k truncation; this makes the practical advantage over embedding-based diffusion (which is 1.75x faster) questionable when quality gains are marginal, and the approach is untested with larger, more realistic vocabularies (e.g., BPE with 50k+ tokens) beyond a small ablation.

The key hyperparameter δ̃ requires task-specific tuning (via grid search in Appendix E) and has a substantial impact on the fluency/diversity trade-off; this adds a non-trivial tuning burden that is not clearly automatable and reduces the practical robustness/plug-and-play nature of the method.

The theoretical motivation rests heavily on the Euclidean semantic space hypothesis applied to a frozen, off-the-shelf BERT embedding matrix, but the paper does not empirically validate that this embedding space actually exhibits the assumed semantic-distance structure (e.g., known anisotropy issues in BERT embeddings are not discussed), leaving the central assumption largely unverified beyond the qualitative example in Appendix L.

No human evaluation is conducted; all quality assessments rely on automatic metrics (MAUVE, BLEU, ROUGE, BERTScore, J-Score) which have well-known limitations for judging fluency and semantic faithfulness, especially given how close many of the compared methods are numerically.

The claimed generalizability to other categorical domains (graphs, protein sequences) is asserted in the introduction and conclusion but never empirically tested, making it a speculative rather than substantiated contribution.

strengths: Clear conceptual contribution: SMOOTHIE unifies two previously disjoint lines of text diffusion (Gaussian embedding diffusion and simplex/categorical diffusion) by smoothing token representations based on semantic distance, and the paper formally proves (Appendix A) that simplex diffusion is a special case of the proposed distance-based space under a trivial metric — a nice theoretical unification.

Theorem 4.1 is a useful practical result: it shows the intractable D0-prediction objective is equivalent (up to a shift-invariant softmax) to a simple embedding-MSE objective, which simplifies training and is proven rigorously in Appendix C.

Extensive empirical evaluation across five diverse tasks (unconditional ROCStories, paraphrase QQP, question generation Quasar-T, summarization XSum, detoxification ParaDetox) plus a large-scale OpenWebText experiment, against a wide range of diffusion and autoregressive baselines.

Controlled ablation isolating the effect of latent space choice: embedding-, simplex-, and smoothing-based diffusion are trained with identical architecture/hyperparameters, which cleanly supports the paper's central claim that the diffusion space itself matters.

Rich set of supporting ablations (δ̃ trade-off, noise scheduler d, embedding choice, self-conditioning, solver comparison, training dynamics, qualitative degradation examples) that substantially aid reproducibility and understanding of the method's behavior.
The proposed non-Markovian sampling solver (Eq. 9) is shown to consistently, if modestly, outperform DDPM/DDIM across all four seq2seq tasks, adding a secondary practical contribution.
Honest and specific limitations section (pretrained vs. end-to-end embeddings, O(V) distance computation cost) rather than generic boilerplate.
weaknesses: Many reported improvements over the strongest baselines (embedding/simplex diffusion, TEncDM, TESS) are numerically small (e.g., BERTScore 68.8 vs 68.2 on XSum, 63.1 vs 63.0 on Quasar-T) and no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed results are reported for most tables, making it hard to assess statistical significance of the claimed 'consistent' superiority.

Results are actually mixed rather than uniformly better: on Quasar-T, SSD-LM/TESS beat SMOOTHIE on ROUGE-L and diversity; on QQP, Embedding* beats SMOOTHIE on BLEU and D-1/4; this tempers the strength of the 'consistently outperforms' claim in the abstract/conclusion.

The justification for why the proposed sampling solver (ignoring the previous latent) outperforms DDPM/DDIM is purely hypothesized ('we hypothesize...', 'a deeper theoretical understanding... is left for future work'), leaving a central empirical claim without solid theoretical grounding.

SMOOTHIE has the same O(batch×seq×d×V) generation-time complexity as simplex diffusion and is 1.75x slower than embedding diffusion; the paper acknowledges this but does not offer or evaluate any mitigation (e.g., approximate/clustered computation), so the practical scalability concern for large vocabularies/long sequences remains open.

All experiments use ~100M-parameter models trained from scratch with a fixed pretrained (frozen) embedding space; the OpenWebText experiment is a partial scaling check but still relatively small-scale and does not include fine-tuned or larger models, leaving generalization to larger, more realistic settings (or fine-tuned embeddings) unverified.

Evaluation relies entirely on automatic metrics (BLEU/ROUGE/BERTScore/MAUVE/J-Score); no human evaluation is conducted to corroborate fluency/coherence claims, which is a common weakness in this literature but still limits confidence in qualitative generation quality conclusions.
